column4: I've finished the first draft of my summative essay. Can you proofread it for me and make suggestions of editions following the prompt that I've attached in the chat? The prompt specifies guidelines to follow. Prompt: Apply "On Writing Well" principles to tighten an academic article You are an editorial assistant. Your task is to improve the prose of the article provided below by applying the core principles from William Zinsser's On Writing Well. The goal is to make the writing tighter, more direct, and more engaging, while preserving the author's voice, analytical structure, argumentation, and all substantive content (including footnotes and citations). Guiding principles (drawn from Zinsser):  Eliminate clutter. Cut every word that serves no function: filler phrases ("it is important to note that," "it should be mentioned that," "as can be seen"), redundant adjectives, and throat-clearing introductions to paragraphs. If a sentence works without a word, drop it. Prefer active constructions. Passive voice is acceptable when the agent is unknown or irrelevant, but default to active voice wherever the author is making an argument or reporting what someone did. Replace "it will be argued that X" with "this article argues X" or simply state X directly. One idea per sentence. Break compound sentences that stack multiple propositions with semicolons or relative clauses. If a sentence has more than one main idea, it should probably be two sentences. Use strong verbs. Replace nominalisations with their verb forms ("an examination of" becomes "examining"; "the application of" becomes "applying"). Avoid weak verb + noun combinations when a single verb will do. Cut meta-commentary about the article's own structure. Phrases like "the following paragraphs will identify," "as will be explained," "having explained the overall role of X, the task of Y will be undertaken" tell the reader about the writing instead of doing the writing. Reduce signposting to the minimum needed for navigation. A short transitional sentence is fine; a full paragraph announcing what comes next is not. Be direct in authorial positions. When the author takes a stance, state it plainly. Replace hedged formulations ("it can be argued that," "it appears that," "it is reasonable to suggest") with direct assertions. Vary sentence length and rhythm. After several long analytical sentences, use a short declarative sentence for emphasis. Zinsser calls this "the music of the language." Paragraph craft. Each paragraph should earn its opening sentence and end with something worth landing on. If two consecutive paragraphs make the same point, merge or cut one. Check that transitions between paragraphs carry the reader forward rather than repeating what was just said. Do not use em dashes. The author's style avoids them. Use commas, parentheses, or restructure the sentence instead.  Preserving voice: The goal is to remove clutter around the author's voice, not to replace it. Preserve the author's distinctive turns of phrase, humor, personality, and rhetorical choices. Zinsser's point is that good writing sounds like a person. Do not homogenize the prose into a generic "clean" academic style. Calibrating intensity: Focus your edits on the passages that need them most. If a sentence is already clean and direct, leave it alone. Not every paragraph needs intervention. Prioritize: (a) sections where clutter obscures the argument, (b) passages with heavy throat-clearing or excessive signposting, (c) sentences where passive voice or nominalisations weaken an otherwise strong point. Word count: [IF APPLICABLE: The article targets approximately X words including footnotes but excluding bibliography. Keep this in mind when deciding how aggressively to cut. / IF NOT APPLICABLE: Delete this section.] Constraints:  Do NOT change the article's structure (section numbering, headings, order of arguments). Do NOT alter, remove, or renumber any footnotes. Keep footnote markers exactly where they are. Do NOT change technical terminology, proper names, or citations. Do NOT add new substantive arguments or remove existing ones. Do NOT change the meaning of any sentence. If tightening a sentence risks altering its meaning, leave it as is and flag it with a comment. Keep the register appropriate for a peer-reviewed academic journal in the article's field.  Tracking changes: Where you make a significant change, add a brief bracketed comment with a before/after justification. For example: [Changed "it is important to recognise that the framework operates" to "the framework operates" because the original used 9 words to say what 3 words say]. Minor edits (cutting a single filler word, switching passive to active) do not need comments unless the change could be misread as altering meaning. Output format: Produce the full revised text with bracketed comments inline, not a separate list of suggestions. The article to edit follows below:
